Hi Alex - great to meet earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our call with your eng/product team:

1) Goals we heard
- Embed Redwood responses into your support UI with structured answers + suggested actions (open ticket, call button)
- Re-rank KB results with embeddings for up-to-date content
- Keep latency under 400ms median for primary flows

2) Integration/arch questions to confirm
- SDK setup & auth: do you prefer server-to-server (service key in your backend) or per-end-user tokens?
- Routing/variants: will you want a fallback model for cost-sensitive paths?
- Structured output/tool calling: you mentioned wanting JSON responses and a small set of callable actions - we recommend function-calling/JSON-schema first-class support.
- Embeddings/rerankers: we should confirm index size and refresh cadence (approx #docs, update frequency).

3) Request/response schema specifics to align on
- Chat vs completions: chat provides role-based messages and is better for multi-turn system/instruction handling; completions can be simpler for single-shot prompts. For structured output and tool-calling, chat + function-calling is the cleanest choice.
- Tokenization & sizing: we usually recommend reserving a safety buffer (200-300 tokens) for model responses when you compute max_tokens. We'll share a token-counting snippet.
- max_tokens/stop: if you need strict JSON-only outputs, we suggest function/JSON schema enforcement or a stop sequence and post-validate.
- Streaming semantics: streaming works well for progressive UI updates (partial answer + finish). If you need strict atomic JSON, stream to the client but assemble/validate server-side before acting on output.

Attachments: I attached a short draft RSP schema (acme-initial-req-resp-draft.json) and our API spec excerpt (ACME_API_Specs.pdf). Vivek - adding your engineering notes below for the tokenization/streaming bits.

Next steps

- If yes, availability for a technical deep-dive Wed/Thu next week (we can include an engineer from our SDK team).

Hi Alex - quick technical notes from our SDK/runtime side (adding context for the PoC):

1) Auth & migration path
- Start with server-side service key (short lived if possible). Recommend using a server-side secret manager and rotating keys monthly. For later per-user tokens, map user_id -> token minted by your auth service and use audience-scoped claims.

2) Chat vs completions & structured output
- Chat API: supports role messages (system, user, assistant) and function-calling / JSON schema enforcement. Use chat + function-calling when you need validated JSON output. That avoids brittle stop-sequence parsing.
- Completions: fine for single-shot text but harder to enforce strict structured outputs.

3) Streaming semantics pattern for deterministic actions
- Stream the human-readable partial text to the client for UX. In parallel, stream tokens to a server-side assembler that reconstructs the final function payload. Only once the function payload validates against the JSON schema do you surface actionable buttons to the user. This gives UX responsiveness and backend reliability.
- Implementation notes: mark stream fragments with sequence ids; include an end-of-function marker. We can provide an SDK helper that returns both an SSE stream and a final assembled object.

4) Tokenization, max_tokens & safety buffer
- Tokenization: our models use byte-pair encoding. Recommend running your typical prompts through our tokenizer during integration to compute the average token footprint.
- max_tokens: compute as (model_max - prompt_tokens - safety_buffer). Start with a 200 token buffer for open-ended answers; for strict JSON responses reduce buffer to ~50-100 and enforce via schema.

5) Embeddings/rerank advice
- Batch embeddings for nightly deltas. Keep an incremental queue to re-embed changed docs. Use an approximate nearest neighbor index (HNSW) with an index refresh strategy: bulk rebuild weekly, apply nightly adds to overlay index to keep latency low.

I attached a tiny SDK snippet with example chat+function call + streaming handler. Happy to walk through the code on the deep-dive.

—Vivek
